verify.one_sentence: GBrain's graph layer buys a real but much smaller win than the README advertises — in the only clean A/B (one switch, shared index and query vectors) typed-edge retrieval adds +6.2 points R@5 and +9.7 points first-place-hit rate on 145 template-matched relationship questions over a 240-page Opus-generated corpus, and the corrected whole-adapter gap is +15.0 P@5 rather than the +31.4 the README still prints — while the BM25+vector fusion layer itself is neutral-to-negative against pure vector search (93.8% vector vs 93.19–93.40% hybrid strict recall_all@5 on the public LongMemEval-S, with vector also leading GBrain's concept and source-swamp fixtures), and the cross-encoder reranker, not the graph and not the fusion, is what supplies the +2.1 points that reach the headline 95.53%.

verify.implications: The claim as put is CONFIRMED — both sentences are verbatim in the same current README, ~395 lines apart — but the reconciliation is asymmetric, and that asymmetry is the finding. (1) They are NOT a contradiction: line 12/379 measures the typed-edge GRAPH on synthetic entity-relationship questions; line 407 measures the BM25+vector FUSION layer on public conversational memory. Different layers, corpora and metrics. The synthesis must say this in one breath (critic C1 closed). (2) But only one of the two numbers survives scrutiny. The LongMemEval sentence is live, on a public third-party benchmark, and its conclusion replicates on three further fixtures (concept search: vector-only 0.6054 nDCG beats both hybrids; source-swamp: 'vector search alone led this fixture'; externally authored questions: vector leads). The +31.4 is a superseded April-2026 whole-system adapter gap, measured with a since-corrected precision denominator on an Opus-written 240-page corpus, whose question generator shares its four templates with the adapter's parser, whose per-query receipts were lost to a gitignored directory (manifest status 'disclosed-gap'), and which GBrain's own corrected re-run puts at +15.0. Both April reports explicitly deny the graph attribution that README line 379 asserts; line 379 also mislabels the comparator (the -31.4 row is the graph-disabled hybrid; vector-only is -38.4). (3) ACTION: four prior reports in this corpus (rag-taxonomy.md, talk-analysis.md, garry-tan-ecosystem.md, projects-built-on-ideas.md) cite +31.4 as the quantitative proof that 'brain > RAG' and must be corrected. Cite instead the isolated one-switch A/B: +6.2 points R@5 and +9.7 points first-place-hit rate, 45 gains and 0 losses across 435 pairs. (4) The honest thesis is narrower but better: typed-edge traversal recovers relational evidence similarity cannot reach (invested_in first-place 9/39 -> 21/39); the fusion layer buys nothing over pure vector; the cross-encoder reranker buys ~2.1 points. This is HippoRAG-adjacent, not novel, and it is a RETRIEVAL result with no answering model in the loop — so the crux question (does curation improve downstream answer accuracy over a tuned BM25+vector baseline?) remains open, exactly as completeness-critic gap 4 says. (5) NO third party has re-executed either number; confidence high, with the caveat that WebSearch budget was exhausted so non-GitHub venues were not swept. Third parties HAVE independently reproduced other GBrain numbers — cotcodec reproduced the memory-conformance cells exactly under hash pinning, aidememo reproduced the baseline band on world-v1, Loringtonian verified the recall_all@5 scorer matches the official evaluator — which is why the correct framing for question (c) is that gbrain-evals is simultaneously the most decision-relevant artifact in the space and the reason to distrust the README above it. (6) Still unresolved and worth flagging: no template-blind paraphrase variant of the relationship questions has ever been run (proposed April 2026 in issue #24), so even the +6.2/+9.7 is measured only on wording the parser was built to recognize.

verify.implications:
FOUR CORRECTIONS REQUIRED. (1) Date: flyfly-recent-identification.md and flyhash-sparse-retrieval.md say "14 June 2026" — change to 8 June 2026. flywire-connectome-simulation.md was correct. (2) Neuron count: delete "~188,000" everywhere; cite 155,916 (paper Fig. 1f) as the headline, noting 158,262 is the live FlyWire Codex figure and ~160,000 was only the expected target. Label which is which — they are not interchangeable. (3) Synapses: delete "199M"; it appears in no primary source. Use 218,460,852 detected synaptic links (18% two-sided) or 3,037,361 neuron-to-neuron connections, and always state which quantity. (4) Dataverse DOI: prior reports cite 10.7910/DVN/8TFGGB, which is the PREPRINT version (CAVE v626); the published version is 10.7910/DVN/7WTH1N (CAVE v888).

CRITIC ITEM C3 IS RESOLVED, and resolved in the direction that DISSOLVES the conflict rather than adjudicating it. There is no BANC-vs-Google contradiction: the two datasets have essentially identical scope (brain + optic lobes + VNC, both missing lamina and ocellar ganglion), and maleCNS at 166,700 genuinely is larger than BANC at ~156-158k. The apparent contradiction existed only because 188,508 — the row count of BANC's metadata table, including 12,750 glia and 37,556 unproofread fragments — had been mistaken for a neuron count. The synthesis should NOT hedge with "probably a scope difference"; it should state plainly that the numbers are compatible.

FOR QUESTION (b), the BANC finding is now citable with exact numbers and is load-bearing for the "distributed control" bridge — but with an important honest caveat the prior reports missed. The paper's own analogy is to Brooks' 1986 SUBSUMPTION ARCHITECTURE in robotics, not to retrieval or memory. Three corrections must flow into the synthesis. (1) Mechanism: the 82/93 pipeline is BM25 -> an LLM candidate-extraction call -> max(serial); the deterministic operator is worth +2 pp pooled and 0 pp at the 262K headline scale. The defensible lesson is "keep version metadata at the granularity at which conflicts occur, and make the resolution policy an explicit, typed, inspectable interface between retrieval and generation" — a schema-and-interface argument, not "replace the model with a database." (2) Framing: "22 published memory systems" is a row count including 6 plain long-context LLMs and 5 plain retrievers; only ~7 are memory systems. Say "the best memory system (HippoRAG-v2) 54%", since GPT-4o long context got 60%. (3) Currency: the "all systems fail" line is stale — MAB v4 has GPT-5-mini at 78 single-hop / 28 multi-hop with no memory layer at all, which is a serious datapoint for the counter-thesis that a big context window plus a reasoning model beats a curation stack on arbitration. Add the caveats when citing: the pipeline is handed the freshness policy a priori (oracle), Mem0/Zep/Cognee/MIRIX ran at 8x coarser chunks than everyone else on this task, ~13 pp of the headline gap is baseline re-implementation drift, published numbers were transcribed not re-run, n=100 per cell, one synthetic MQUAKE dataset with ~2 candidates per conflict, and the LongMemEval transfer is a null result (p=0.45). The Zep/Graphiti datapoint (7% FC-SH, its lowest column, vs BM25's 48%) is still worth keeping as a caution about memory-vendor invalidation claims, but it must carry the chunk-4096 caveat. For the company-brain design answer, this shifts the recommendation from "put arbitration in Postgres" to "store a version/valid-time key per fact, extract candidates into a typed structure before deciding, and expose the resolution policy as swappable code (newest, second-newest, aggregate) — because the LongMemEval failures show a single max() is not enough."

evidence.fact: MemConflict formalizes three conflict types: dynamic (later state supersedes — recency wins), static (a later mention contradicts an invariant fact and is FALSE — recency is inverted), and conditional (multiple values each true under their own condition — recency is undefined). Static conflicts are built only over invariant attributes and "the later mention at s_q is explicitly treated as false information rather than as a valid state update"; conditional values "are factually correct and do not represent temporal updates of one another." So newest-wins is the correct policy for 1 of 3 types.

MemConflict Table 3, six memory systems: best static Answer Accuracy 0.4375 (MemOS), best conditional 0.8449 (MemOS), best dynamic 0.4966 (LangMem). LangMem is best on dynamic but worst on conditional (0.1556) — the profile of a system that over-applies supersession. Conflict Recognition Score is at most 0.2501 for every system: systems rarely even detect that a contradiction exists. "Across most systems and conflict types, retrieval failures account for the dominant share of errors."

ConflictRAG source-selection accuracy against human ground truth (200 factual samples, kappa=0.79): Entropy-TOPSIS (data-derived weights over LLM-extracted scores) 82.7%, LLM direct selection 78.3%, fixed (hand-specified) weights 75.6%, equal weights 71.2%, random 53.4%. A hand-written deterministic rule is 2.7 points WORSE than just asking the LLM. Entropy weights rank authority 0.312 above recency 0.245.

ConflictRAG types conflicts as factual/temporal/opinion, each with a distinct resolution strategy (only temporal uses recency ranking, over "metadata or LLM-extracted dates"). Four-class type classification reaches only 74.3% accuracy; ablating the classifier so everything defaults to the factual strategy costs -7.9% correctness, and removing conflict detection costs -16.6%, at which point "the system approaches standard RAG+Reranking performance."

RegDivergence-101 (FDA vs EMA guidance pairs, expert-grounded, dual-annotation kappa=0.85, n=101): lexical heuristic 0.511 macro-F1 [0.411-0.605], NLI cross-encoder 0.233, obligation-level Graph-RAG 0.663 [0.570-0.747], flat LLM judge (Claude Haiku) 0.830 [0.747-0.908]. On a real expert-annotated contradiction corpus the LLM judge beats the deterministic heuristic by 32 points with non-overlapping CIs. The SILENT label (one source says nothing) is "semantically detectable but invisible to entailment-only formulations" and has no ordering key at all.

German statutory QA benchmark, 312 expert-validated time-sensitive pairs: 113 Pre-Amendment + 84 Multi-Provision Pre-Amendment = 197 (63%) require the OLDER version because the fact pattern is historically anchored, so max(serial) is wrong on 63% of the benchmark. What works is deterministic as-of-time filtering (regex extracts the as-of date from the query, then hard-filters to versions valid then): RAG-ToC 0.48-0.83 and RAG-kNN 0.54-0.81 vs Vanilla 0.37-0.54; Claude Opus 4.5 goes 35.40% to 81.42%. Web search "exhibits a marked recency bias on historically anchored tasks" (+0.20-0.24, p<0.05, only in the Web condition).

Of 697 LLM-generated statutory QA candidate pairs, only 312 (44.8%) survived review by two senior law students and a qualified lawyer; the leading rejection reasons were that "the version change was only editorial in nature rather than substantive" and that "the legal consequence remained identical regardless of which version was applied." Even on a corpus with formal version-validity intervals, distinguishing substantive supersession from editorial revision required human semantic judgment more than half the time.

ContextConflict (EMNLP 2026) defines six contextual conflict types over 5,781 samples — misinformation 1,004, inferential 787, temporal 960 (16.6%), granularity 1,020, perspective 1,010, ambiguity 1,000 — so recency is the right policy for 1 of 6, and three of the six (ambiguity, perspective, granularity) have no single winner at all, the correct output being a balanced summary preserving divergent viewpoints.

ContextConflict's temporal split had to have its ordering key manufactured: ConflictBank-temporal instances carry only "an implicit chronological order", so "We attach an explicit timestamp to each statement... so that temporal relationships become unambiguous. Because timestamps can change gold labels, each instance is verified by two independent annotators with discussion-based adjudication." Even after explicit timestamps are supplied, 93.5% of temporal instances are "implicit" (needing >=2 inferential steps) and the best of seven models reaches only 68.0% accuracy.

MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation supplies both the ordering key and the answer: every sentence carries an integer serial (larger = newer) and the resolution rule is printed verbatim in the agent's prompt ("the newer fact has larger serial number. You need to solve the conflicts... by finding the newest fact"), with a candidate set that "generally caps at an original and one counterfactual value." max(serial) is the answer key transcribed into Python, not a discovered solution.

GBrain, the reference company-brain implementation, does the opposite of the inference: `gbrain eval suspected-contradictions` applies a deterministic >30-day date pre-filter and then runs an LLM judge (claude-haiku-4-5) emitting one of six verdicts — no_contradiction / contradiction / temporal_supersession / temporal_regression / temporal_evolution / negation_artifact — reports rates with a Wilson 95% CI, and never mutates the brain, emitting paste-ready resolution commands for a human. Four of the six verdicts are distinctions a serial number cannot make.

The freshness paper's own README states the determinism "earns its place on systems grounds (a known policy becomes exact, inspectable, and independently testable), not on average accuracy" — holding extraction and T=0 fixed and swapping the LLM policy executor for Python max() is worth +2.0 pp pooled and 0.0 pp at the headline 262K scale.

verify.implications:
The synthesis must NOT say "contradiction arbitration belongs in deterministic code, not an LLM judge." Replace it with a two-part split: deterministic code owns ELIGIBILITY and BOOKKEEPING (valid-from/valid-until intervals, source attribution, applicability conditions, ACL/scope filters, and an as-of-date filter applied BEFORE arbitration — worth 35%->81% on historically anchored statutory questions); the model owns ADJUDICATION (which kind of disagreement this is — supersession, regression, evolution, scoped exception, or parsing artifact — and therefore which policy applies); a human owns contested resolution.

Three concrete consequences for the synthesis and for design question (b):

1. READ PATH — the conclusion survives, on narrower grounds. Do not put a lexical shingle FlyHash in front of an embedding index. But the true general principle is simply that no hash of an embedding beats the embedding; hashing is a compression/speed trade, so FlyHash competes with LSH / ITQ / PQ / binary quantization, never with the dense vector. H3D should be cited as evidence that a ~40-bit lexical fingerprint is a poor semantic index, NOT as evidence that the fly algorithm is unsuitable.

2. WRITE PATH — the sweep's decision (i) (FlyHash/fly-Bloom-filter novelty gate + dedup at ingest) is NOT damaged by H3D and must stop being hedged with the 0.13-vs-0.34 number, which is about a different task. H3D provides no near-duplicate benchmark; its dedup evidence is a 3-document toy where every method scores 1.00. The gate remains unproven in both directions.

3. DESIGN SPEC — if the design panel proposes a fly-derived ingest gate, it must apply k-WTA on top of the embedding already computed (m >> d expansion, ~5% activity, Dasgupta's actual regime, where Ryali et al. show 10-37x gains over classical LSH at short code lengths), not on shingles. That exact cell (BGE embedding -> FlyHash) is the one H3D leaves empty — unclaimed ground and a cheap crux experiment: run FlyHash-on-BGE on CSFCube/RELISH against BGE-LSHash and BGE-BIHash. Any such proposal must also be costed against MinHashLSH and modern binary/int8 embedding quantization, neither of which H3D covers at strength; on H3D's own turf the boring winner among fixed-rule lexical hashes is Winnowing+Jaccard, not FlyHash. pgvector documented storage: vector = 4*dims+8 B (1536-d = 6,152 B), halfvec = 2*dims+8 B, bit = dims/8+8 B (1536-d = 200 B, a 30.8x reduction). Estimated HNSW index size at d=1536, m=16: 100K chunks = 599 MiB float32 / 31 MiB binary; 1M = 5.85 GiB / 313 MiB; 10M = 58.5 GiB / 3.05 GiB. Memory is not a constraint at company-brain scale.

At 10x expansion it is still 1,920 B.

pgvector indexes sparsevec with HNSW only up to 1,000 non-zero elements. A 40x-expansion FlyHash code (3,072 nnz) cannot be indexed at all; a 10x code (768 nnz) costs 8*768+16 = 6,160 B per row, exactly the size of the float32 vector, for worse recall. Shipping FlyHash in GBrain requires writing a new access method.

verify.implications:
Three changes to the final answer, one of them a reversal of a prior finding.

1. REVERSAL — the corpus's fallback position is wrong. Every fly report in findings/ concedes the index role and retreats to "FlyHash as a write-side dedup gate." That retreat is not defensible either: on H3D, the only benchmark that runs these methods side by side, SimHash beats FlyHash on BOTH datasets on BOTH quality and time (CSFCube 0.1770 vs 0.1325 at 3.62 s vs 10.95 s; RELISH 0.4756 at 0.00 s vs 0.4305 at 1744 s), and MinHash and Winnowing beat it on quality. Checkpoint 01's decision (i) — "write-side: FlyHash/fly-Bloom-filter novelty gate + dedup at ingest" — must be split: the dedup half is refuted, the novelty half survives. SYNTHESIS.md should say "fly Bloom filter as a novelty/staleness clock," never "FlyHash for dedup."

2. The critic's gap 5 is closed with a harder answer than expected. The arithmetic does not merely show FlyHash is unnecessary — it shows FlyHash is counterproductive. At d=1536 with the fly's own 40x expansion, the code is 7,680 B, larger than the 6,152 B float32 vector and 38x larger than binary quantization's 200 B; and pgvector cannot HNSW-index a sparsevec above 1,000 non-zeros, so the fly's parameters do not fit GBrain's actual database. Meanwhile a 1M-chunk HNSW index is 5.85 GiB (313 MiB binary-quantized) and DiskANN serves a BILLION points at <3 ms on one 64 GB box. The memory motivation for FlyHash-as-index is dead by two independent arguments.

3. The three "unique" FlyHash selling points are each matched by an incumbent already in the stack. Data-independent/no-training: HNSW has no training step (pgvector's own words) and binary_quantize() is a deterministic sign function. Streaming inserts, no rebuild: same. Sparse codes in an inverted index: SPLADE++ scores 50.5 BEIR nDCG@10 vs BM25's 43.7 within 4 ms of BM25 latency, and fits pgvector sparsevec today. So the steelman FOR FlyHash collapses to exactly one non-duplicated property — the fly Bloom filter's AIMD time-decay, which gives duplication and staleness in one number with O(1) state — and even that has never been measured against the free baseline (one ANN probe for max-cosine against the index you already built) or against SAGE's published vMF gate.

For question (b) "can it be combined with fruit-fly brain work": the honest answer narrows to one buildable, testable proposal — a fly Bloom filter novelty/staleness gate in front of put_page — with ~30% confidence it beats the free baseline, plus a named crux experiment (Arm B in the report) whose outcome is genuinely unknown. Everything else on the fly-algorithm side should be presented as refuted, not as promising-but-unproven. Two design-panel implications: any d1–d5 design doc proposing FlyHash as a vector.backend should be dropped, and the design that survives should benchmark the fly gate against SAGE and against 64-bit simhash, not against a plain Bloom filter as the PNAS paper did.

Caveat to carry forward: the literal experiment (FlyHash applied on top of BGE/E5 embeddings versus binary_quantize + rescoring) still has not been run by anyone; I found only the nearest proxy (H3D's BGE-LSHash), which points the same way. And H3D itself contains one visibly broken row (MinHash+mahalanobis, NDCG@20 = 1.0000), so cite it as strong-but-single-source.

key_insights: Bi-temporality is 40-year-old database prior art, standardised in SQL:2011 and shipping in Db2, MariaDB, SQL Server (transaction-time only), XTDB, Oracle. The three prior reports' intervention #1 is the standard's application-time period + system-time period, and they cite none of it.

The piece every agent-memory system skips is not the two timestamps — it is the CONSTRAINT. SQL:2011's `PRIMARY KEY (key, period WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` turns 'two contradictory live facts' from a retrieval problem a nightly probe discovers into a write-time constraint violation the database refuses. Zep/Graphiti, GBrain, and every system surveyed store the timestamps and enforce nothing.

What LLM-era systems genuinely add over SQL:2011 is exactly two things: an extractor that manufactures the (subject, predicate, object, valid_from) key out of prose, and a semantic candidate-retrieval step that finds WHICH stored row a new claim might contradict (SQL cannot look up a key that does not exist yet). Everything downstream is `UPDATE ... FOR PORTION OF`. Graphiti's arbitration is 31 lines of interval arithmetic with no model call.

Supersession vs contradiction vs debate is decidable from the schema with zero model calls: same (subject,predicate) + DISJOINT valid intervals = supersession (trim, no judge); + OVERLAPPING + same holder = contradiction (run policy, log judge, retain loser); + OVERLAPPING + different holder = debate (legal by construction). The line between the first two is overlap; between the last two is the holder column.

'Debate' is the escape hatch that keeps the invariant true: when the conflict policy cannot pick a winner, re-key the loser's holder from 'org' to 'source:crm'. The overlap constraint is satisfied (holders differ), nothing is dropped, retrieval labels the disagreement honestly. GBrain's docs say it cannot currently mint this state.

GBrain is uni-temporal with an audit stamp, not bitemporal, despite migration v122's own inline comment claiming 'facts already gives bi-temporal validity'. valid_from/valid_until/expired_at are all valid-time or tombstones; there is no transaction-time END column, so 'what did we believe on date D' is unanswerable from SQL.

A concrete cross-cycle supersession failure follows from three individually reasonable lines in consolidate.ts: the scan filters `consolidated_at IS NULL`, every cluster member is then marked consolidated, and the newest fact in each cluster keeps valid_until = NULL. Tomorrow's contradicting fact is clustered only against other unconsolidated facts, never meets yesterday's winner, and the brain ends up holding two current facts about the same entity with different values — and no constraint objects.

GBrain's transaction-time axis does exist — in git, not Postgres. The repo is the system of record and the DB a derived cache, so commit time IS the system period. That is Dolt's architecture with version control outside the database. Caveats: not joinable in SQL, and page-granular rather than claim-granular.

The bitemporal claim ledger the three prior reports want is structurally the UNION of GBrain's two existing tables: facts' timestamps and enforced NOT NULL provenance, plus takes' holder and weight, under one exclusion constraint. The substrate is already built and split across the hot/cold seam.

PostgreSQL 18 (2025-09-25) added the constraint half of SQL:2011 (WITHOUT OVERLAPS, FOREIGN KEY ... PERIOD) but NOT system versioning — zero occurrences of `FOR SYSTEM_TIME` or `WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING` in its release notes or CREATE TABLE reference. On GBrain's stack you get the constraint natively and must hand-roll close-and-reinsert for transaction time.

key_facts.claim: SQL:2011 defines valid time as 'the time period during which a row is regarded as correctly reflecting reality by the user of the database' and transaction time as 'the time period during which a row is committed to or recorded in the database'; valid time is provided by application-time period tables, transaction time by system-versioned tables, and a table may be both (bitemporal).

SQL:2011's answer to two contradictory live facts is a constraint, not a probe: `ALTER TABLE Emp ADD PRIMARY KEY (ENo, EPeriod WITHOUT OVERLAPS)`, motivated in the paper by exactly the company-brain case (an employee appearing to belong to two departments over overlapping periods). Temporal referential integrity is `FOREIGN KEY (EDept, PERIOD EPeriod) REFERENCES Dept (DNo, PERIOD DPeriod)`.

The bitemporal 'what did we believe on date D' query in the standard is `SELECT ENo, EDept FROM Emp FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF TIMESTAMP '2011-07-01 00:00:00' WHERE ENo = 22217 AND EPeriod CONTAINS DATE '2010-12-01'` — 'the department where the employee worked as of December 1, 2010, recorded in the database as of July 1, 2011'. Two dates, two axes, one query.

TSQL2's committee formed July 1993 (Snodgrass chairing, 19 members incl. Kulkarni and Jensen); the SQL committee's temporal project was 'eventually cancelled around 2001'. TSQL2 lost on hidden period columns and statement modifiers whose semantics were underspecified — the transferable lesson being that a memory system must not hide 'current' behind implicit query rewriting.

PostgreSQL 18 (released 2025-09-25) added temporal constraints: 'WITHOUT OVERLAPS for PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE, and PERIOD for foreign keys'. `UNIQUE (id, valid_at WITHOUT OVERLAPS)` behaves like `EXCLUDE USING GIST (id WITH =, valid_at WITH &&)`, requires a range/multirange column, and needs the btree_gist extension for the equality columns.

PostgreSQL 18 has NO system versioning: zero occurrences of 'WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING' or 'FOR SYSTEM_TIME' in its release notes or CREATE TABLE reference. Transaction time on Postgres must be hand-rolled (trigger, the `periods` extension, or explicit close-and-reinsert).

SQL Server's temporal tables are system-versioned ONLY — 'Temporal tables (also known as system-versioned temporal tables)' — with five FOR SYSTEM_TIME subclauses (AS OF, FROM...TO, BETWEEN...AND, CONTAINED IN, ALL) and no application-time support. MariaDB has all three shapes with standard syntax.

XTDB v2 is bitemporal by default with four automatic columns _valid_from/_valid_to/_system_from/_system_to, 'all data is bitemporal without having to think about storing or updating additional columns', with SQL 'built to reflect the SQL:2011 standard' and supporting FOR VALID_TIME AS OF / ALL and SETTING DEFAULT SYSTEM_TIME TO AS OF.

Datomic is transaction-time only (as-of / since / history over :db/txInstant; a datom is an immutable five-tuple where retraction is an assertion with Op=false); valid time must be modelled as a user attribute. Dolt is likewise transaction-time only, using git commits as the axis: 'Dolt SQL supports a variant of SQL 2011 syntax to query non-HEAD revisions via the AS OF clause'.

Graphiti's EntityEdge carries exactly four timestamps mapping 1:1 onto SQL:2011 — created_at/expired_at ('when the node was invalidated') = system period, valid_at ('when the fact became true')/invalid_at ('when the fact stopped being true') = valid period.

Graphiti's arbitration (resolve_edge_contradictions, edge_operations.py:538-571) is 31 lines of pure interval arithmetic with no model call, and invalidates only when `edge.valid_at < resolved_edge.valid_at` strictly. If the incoming claim is BACKDATED (valid_at earlier than or equal to the stored edge) or either valid_at is None, no branch fires and both contradictory edges stay live — with no overlap constraint to catch it.

TOKI (arXiv:2606.06240, Ziming Wang, 2026-06-04) frames the problem as 'contradiction resolution is write-time concurrency control', types four production heuristics (last-writer-wins, evidence-weighted merge, await-confirmation, per-rule policy) as bitemporal operators over a dual-row schema, preserves losing facts in audit rows, and proves that 'keyed logging of the adjudicating judge is necessary for replay consistency, which every audited baseline omits'.

TOKI's verdict matrix over eight systems: 'every baseline that keeps a language-model judge on the write path admits at least one of three write-time anomalies (replay inconsistency, belief-drift skew, audit erasure); a content-addressed engine-layer comparator avoids them only by removing the judge, and TOKI alone excludes all three while keeping it.' Reported: LoCoMo audit-row defence moves score by 0.86; removing the typed memory layer costs 0.49 accuracy on 1,444 answerable questions.

GBrain's facts table (migrate.ts:2384) has valid_from TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, valid_until TIMESTAMPTZ, expired_at, superseded_by BIGINT REFERENCES facts(id), created_at, and source TEXT NOT NULL — but no transaction-time END column. All three of valid_from/valid_until/expired_at are valid-time or tombstones, so migration v122's inline comment claiming 'facts already gives bi-temporal validity' overstates: the table is an application-time period table with a creation stamp.

Neither migrate.ts nor the 1,618-line schema.sql contains any occurrence of EXCLUDE USING, tstzrange, daterange, WITHOUT OVERLAPS or btree_gist. Nothing prevents two live facts with the same entity_slug+dimension and different values; the only uniqueness is idx_facts_ontology_dedup, a value_hash dedup index, not an overlap constraint. facts also lacks the CHECK (valid_until > valid_from) that SQL:2011 says a period definition implies.

Cross-cycle supersession fails in GBrain: consolidate scans only `consolidated_at IS NULL` facts (consolidate.ts:68-78), marks every cluster member consolidated (:241-244), and leaves the newest fact per cluster with valid_until = NULL (:246-273). Tomorrow's contradicting fact clusters only against other unconsolidated facts and never meets yesterday's winner, leaving two current facts about the same entity with different values.

GBrain's automatic arbitration key is recency within a greedy cosine cluster at threshold 0.85 with minFactsPerBucket 3 (consolidate.ts:52-55) — i.e. semantic similarity, the exact discriminator MemStrata measured at AUROC 0.59 for separating contradiction from paraphrase. Migration v122 already ships the right key unused: dimension + value_hash keyed on (source_id, entity_slug, dimension).

GBrain detects rather than prevents: the probe 'never mutates the brain', emits paste-ready resolution_commands with a six-verdict enum (no_contradiction | contradiction | temporal_supersession | temporal_regression | temporal_evolution | negation_artifact) and a Wilson 95% CI, and 'a mark-as-debate subcommand does not exist yet' — so the third state (intentional disagreement) cannot be represented in the hot layer at all.

GBrain's eval_contradictions_cache keys on (chunk_a_hash, chunk_b_hash, model, prompt_version, truncation_policy) — which IS the keyed judge logging TOKI proves is necessary for replay consistency — but it lives in an eval table and is not joinable to the fact rows it adjudicated.

The `periods` PostgreSQL extension reimplements SQL:2011 periods AND `WITH SYSTEM VERSIONING` via functions/views/triggers for PG 9.5-15; `temporal_tables` supports 'system-period temporal tables only'. Both cite Snodgrass's 1999 book as the reference text.

gaps.recommendation: Rewrite intervention #1 in the synthesis as: "adopt SQL:2011 bitemporal tables with a WITHOUT OVERLAPS constraint" — not "add bi-temporal invalidation." The rhetorical framing matters because the recommendation is currently vulnerable to a database engineer's first objection, and the fix is a citation plus one structural upgrade: the value is in the CONSTRAINT (make contradiction unrepresentable at write time), not in the timestamps (which everyone already has and nobody enforces). Include in the synthesis: (1) the valid-time vs transaction-time definitions verbatim from Kulkarni & Michels 2012, (2) the three-way supersession/contradiction/debate decision table — overlap separates the first two, holder separates the last two, no model call needed — as the cleanest statement of "who arbitrates when facts disagree" from Tan's talk, (3) TOKI (arXiv:2606.06240) as the paper that closes this gap in the agent-memory literature, framed as "contradiction resolution is write-time concurrency control," and (4) the honest delta: what Zep/Graphiti and GBrain add over 2011 is the extractor that manufactures the key from prose and the semantic candidate search — not the temporal model. On GBrain specifically, report it as uni-temporal-with-an-audit-stamp (correcting migration v122's own comment), credit git as its real transaction-time axis (Dolt's architecture, version control outside the DB), and lead the recommendations with the two cheap wins: a CHECK (valid_until > valid_from), and a partial GiST exclusion constraint on (source_id, entity_slug, dimension) over the valid range — which converts the verified cross-cycle supersession failure into a write error at the one moment the evidence for arbitrating it is still in context. Flag two things before anyone plans work: btree_gist availability under PGLite is unverified (low confidence, likely absent, which would force a trigger for the WASM engine), and TOKI's benchmark numbers are abstract-only.

key_insights: The ANN index is NOT the bottleneck, settled by measurement, not estimate. I built real pgvector 0.8.6 HNSW indexes locally today: a top-10 query over 250,000 x 1024-dim vectors returns in 10.7 ms (3.8 ms at 100K). GBrain's own published `gbrain search` median is 122 ms, its reranker adds +150 ms p50, and a synthesized answer is ~3 s dominated by the Anthropic API. The ANN scan is ~3.7% of retrieval latency and ~0.14% of an answered question. A FlyHash index that was free, instant AND lossless would improve an answered question by at most 0.14% — so FlyHash-as-the-semantic-index is dead on arithmetic, independent of the H3D quality evidence (0.13 vs 0.34 MAP). Only the write-side fly Bloom filter / novelty gate survives, because it acts on the curation path where 99%+ of the money is.

Cost is dominated by write-side LLM curation, by 222x-4,514x. GBrain's own receipt: takes extraction = $0.0128/page actual ($0.033 quoted, $0.260 at Opus-class). Embedding the same page = $0.0000576. GBrain's `docs/operations/spend-controls.md` opens by saying 'GBrain itself is rounding error; the spend that matters is downstream embedding' — its own receipts invert that by ~222x, and every spend gate in that doc except one guards the cheap side.

Tan's 'under $100/month for a 25-person company' is PARTIALLY CONFIRMED — right answer, wrong arithmetic, dominant cost out of scope. The $100 ceiling does hold for GBrain's own AI spend up to ~10 new pages/person/day ($88.74/mo). But both stated halves are wrong: '$40/mo embeddings' implies 694,444 new pages/month (1,263 per person per working day) or 4.5 full re-embeds of the whole brain monthly — the real figure is $0.03-$0.63/mo, and plausibly $0.00 inside Voyage's 200M free-token grant. The omitted nightly dream cycle is the actual dominant brain-side line. The errors partially cancel, which is why the headline survives. 'Plus your hosting bill' hides $135/mo minimum — more than the entire AI budget it is appended to. And the agent loop that consumes the brain is excluded: GBrain's own anchor is ~$700/mo for ONE power user, i.e. 18-175x the whole claim at 25 seats.

1,024 dimensions is the single worst choice in pgvector, and it is GBrain's new-install default. Measured and confirmed three times to the byte: 1024-d and 1536-d cost EXACTLY the same 8,192 bytes/vector of HNSW index, while 768-d costs 4,096. A 1024-d element wastes 46% of every 8 KB index page because only one fits. GBrain's move from 1536-d to 1024-d bought zero index-size reduction. `halfvec(1024)` would cut the index 3x (8,192 -> 2,731 B/vec) with one DDL change, dropping a 1M-page brain from a $410/mo Supabase 2XL to a $210/mo XL. The index sets the hosting tier, not the latency — and the right fixes are halfvec, binary quantization, or the pgvectorscale proposal already in the repo, none of which is FlyHash.
