key_insights: The objection is ~70% right. During 2026 the incumbents closed three of the seven requirements that looked like Tan's differentiators: skills (Glean imports SKILL.md from GitHub under the open Agent Skills standard; Notion saves skills AS SKILL.md; Dust ships nightly 'Self Improving Skills' that propose evidence-based diffs for human approval = GBrain's skillopt shipped by a competitor), write-side curation (Guru automatically verifies AND unverifies knowledge from behavioral signals and excludes unverified content from answers), and agent-facing MCP (universal; Microsoft's federated connectors ARE MCP servers).

The remaining 30% traces to one architectural fork: every incumbent is an INDEX OVER SOURCES (the source app stays authoritative, the index is a disposable projection), while a GBrain-style brain is a NEW SYSTEM OF RECORD (git markdown) the agent writes to. Everything follows from this. Incumbents inherit ACLs, retention and deletion for free but structurally CANNOT curate (they can only nudge a human to fix the doc in the source app); brains get curation for free and must invent governance from scratch. You cannot decay or supersede a fact you do not own.

Contradiction arbitration (R4) is genuinely unclaimed ground, verified by exhaustive grep of vendors' own doc indexes: 0 of 1,402 Glean doc pages mention 'contradict'; 0 hits in the public MicrosoftDocs/microsoft-365-docs repo; 0 in Dust's llms.txt; Guru's own quality page does not claim it. This is not oversight — an index-over-sources product has no authority to resolve a conflict between two source documents, so returning both IS its correct behavior.

Every incumbent 'memory' shipped in 2026 is PER-USER personalization, not organizational memory: Glean ('does not share memory data across users'), Microsoft (hidden folder in the user's Exchange mailbox), Dust ('private to each user'). Tan's R3 — a SHARED hot facts tier consolidating into a shared cold takes layer with multi-holder epistemics — is different in kind and unmatched in this comparison set. It is also where the ACL problem bites hardest, because a shared hot tier is a shared blast radius.

The ACL gap is real but must be stated at the right granularity, and Tan states it himself: GBrain's company-brain scoping is SOURCE-granular via per-teammate OAuth clients (--source/--federated-read, SQL-enforced), and docs/tutorials/company-brain.md says 'Read scoping stays source-granular in both models — within a shared source, everyone entitled to the source can read every folder.' Glean/Copilot/Rovo mirror per-DOCUMENT ACLs from the source system and evaluate per-user at query time. That is a category difference, not a maturity gap.

Onyx is the honest calibration on how expensive permission mirroring is: permission sync exists for only 11 of ~52 connectors, is Enterprise-Edition-only, and runs on 5–30 minute polling intervals (ACLs eventually consistent with a measurable staleness window). 'Just add ACLs to GBrain' is not a sprint — it is a per-connector fleet that even funded incumbents cover at ~21%.

Governance failure is not one-sided: Microsoft's own docs state that Purview retention policies and labels DO NOT apply to Copilot memory, that memory actions generate NO Purview audit log entries, and that admins cannot restrict what enters memory. The moment even Microsoft added a derived agent-written store, it fell outside the retention and audit plane. Agent-written memory is an unsolved governance category industry-wide — a more defensible framing than 'Tan forgot about ACLs'.

What a company brain actually adds, ranked: (1) per-fact provenance + temporal validity in an owned, diffable store (source is NOT NULL; remember errors provenance_required) — incumbents have per-DOCUMENT citations, a weaker guarantee; (2) contradiction detection that refuses to auto-resolve; (3) a shared org-scoped hot→cold consolidation loop; (4) ownership and exit (MIT, markdown, git, a frozen MEMORY_VERBS v1 protocol with a conformance harness) — the one item an incumbent structurally cannot copy. Skills and MCP are struck from the list.

The differentiator window is narrow and closing: Glean already imports skills from GitHub and mirrors ACLs; nothing in its architecture prevents it shipping per-fact provenance and a contradiction probe in a single release, which would collapse items 1–3 and leave only ownership/exit. This is the strongest counter-argument to the report's own conclusion and should be carried into the synthesis.

Nobody on either side has run the crux experiment: same corpus, same top-k, same reranker, Glean/Onyx-class hybrid retrieval vs a curated brain, scored specifically on knowledge-update and conflict question slices. The thesis predicts incumbents fail on exactly those two slices and tie elsewhere. It is cheap on LongMemEval-S's knowledge-update split and would settle the debate.

key_facts.claim: Glean Skills 'follow the open Agent Skills standard'; a SKILL.md can be imported directly from a public or private GitHub repository root, subtree path, or direct file link, and Glean 'records the source so the Skill can stay in sync with upstream changes'. Automatic Skill routing evaluates queries against Skill descriptions.

Zero of the 1,402 documentation entries in Glean's llms.txt index mention 'contradict' or contradiction detection. Glean ships Sensitive Findings scanning, Access verification and an agent development lifecycle, but no facility for noticing that two indexed documents disagree.

Glean mirrors source permissions: 'When a connector crawls content, it also ingests the permission model from that source (ACLs, group memberships, role assignments). At query time, Glean evaluates the signed-in user's identity against those mirrored permissions before returning any results' — enforced uniformly across search, AI answers, agents, MCP servers and embedded integrations, with explicit 'No privilege escalation'.

Glean's Indexing API models pushed-document permissions with allowAnonymousAccess, allowedUsers, allowAllDatasourceUsersAccess and allowedGroups; users/groups must be indexed first, permissions apply asynchronously, and /checkdocumentaccess validates them.

Glean memory is strictly per-user: 'Glean stores memory data at the individual user level and does not share memory data across users' and 'memory doesn't create cross-company or cross-user learning'. Saved memories persist until deleted; extracted memories are 'living, versioned records' that 'age out gradually'.

Glean Verification is human-driven write-side curation: a green badge showing who verified and when, a Tasks queue of verification requests, and re-verify reminders that return the document to the owner's task list.

Onyx's permission sync covers only 11 real sources (Google Drive, Confluence, Jira, Canvas, Box, Slack, Gmail, GitHub, Salesforce, Teams, SharePoint) plus a mock connector, out of ~52 connector packages in backend/onyx/connectors.

Onyx permission-sync intervals are 5 minutes by default and 30 minutes for Confluence, Jira, Canvas, Box and SharePoint document sync — so mirrored ACLs are eventually consistent with a 5–30 minute staleness window.
Onyx states 'Onyx's context retrieval respects user level permissions which is only configurable via the Enterprise Edition' — permission enforcement is not in the MIT Community Edition.

Dust ships Self Improving Skills: 'Every night, Dust analyzes user conversations that make use of skills', using explicit thumbs feedback and implicit signals ('a user correcting the agent's output, a tool that failed to be invoked when it should have been, a conversation that went off track'), then surfaces syntax-highlighted diffs that skill editors Approve or Decline — 'Nothing is applied to your skill without your explicit approval.'

Dust's access model is Spaces-granular, not document-granular: admins 'Create dedicated spaces (open or restricted)' and 'Segregate company data between open and restricted spaces'; users interact with agents built on the data of spaces they are a member of. It does not mirror per-document source ACLs per user.

Dust Agent Memory is per-user: 'Memories are private to each user and only you can view and manage your memories with each agent... each agent maintains separate memory spaces for complete isolation of your data.'

Microsoft 365 Copilot supports two connector models: synced connectors that ingest and semantically index content into Microsoft Graph, and federated connectors that 'retrieve content in real time by using Model Context Protocol (MCP) without indexing data into Microsoft Graph'. More than 100 connectors are available.

Microsoft 365 Copilot grounding is ACL-scoped: 'Operating inside the Microsoft 365 service boundary doesn't grant Copilot tenant-wide visibility. Data access is always scoped to the signed-in user's permissions', and Copilot honors Conditional Access and MFA.

Copilot memory is per-user, stored 'in the user's Exchange mailbox in a hidden folder'. Critically: 'Retention policies and retention labels configured in Purview by organization admins don't apply to Copilot memory... There are no admin controls to enforce retention rules specifically for Copilot memory', 'Memory and personalization actions don't generate audit log entries in Purview', and admins 'can't restrict what type of information is added to Copilot memory'.
Atlassian's Teamwork Graph offers '100 out-of-the-box connectors' and 'runs last-mile checks, so users and apps only get access to the data they're entitled to'.

Rovo agents execute with the invoking user's permissions: 'the agent is acting on that person's behalf. It therefore can only return or interact with spaces, pages, work items, and other information that the user has permission to access... If the user can't comment, the agent can't comment.' Studio admins can restrict agent creation to All users / Selected groups (max 10) / No users.

Guru ships the most automated write-side curation in the incumbent set: 'Automatically verify and unverify knowledge—so your AI and your teams always work from what's accurate', driven by 'behavioral signals — usage, views, feedback, and expert interactions'; every decision is logged with a stated reason and a confidence level, and unverified content 'can be automatically excluded from answers and search results'.

Notion Skills are markdown: 'Notion saves the skill as a SKILL.md file, along with any files attached to the skill that are approved to share.' Skills are written and maintained as Notion pages, invoked by slash command or automatically by Notion Agent, and versioned via page history.

GBrain's own company-brain tutorial states the ACL limit explicitly: 'Read scoping stays source-granular in both models — within a shared source, everyone entitled to the source can read every folder.' Scoping is per-teammate OAuth clients with --source and --federated-read (SQL-enforced), plus optional write binding via --bound-slug-prefixes.

GBrain's schema.sql line 24 documents access_policy as a 'forward-compat slot, no enforcement in v0.17', and its RLS block (lines 1563–1616) notes 'The postgres role (used by gbrain via pooler) has BYPASSRLS' — RLS blocks anonymous access rather than enforcing per-user document ACLs. The shipped ACCESS_POLICY.md template is prose 'read by the agent before every response', deferring runtime MCP enforcement to TODOS.md.

Slite Ask has verified-doc filtering ('Filter the sources to make sure that you can trust the answers with verified docs'), identifies knowledge gaps, and is permission-filtered: 'Ask accesses only those docs you can view, filtering team workspace content by your permissions.'

Coda Brain could not be assessed: coda.io/product/coda-brain now 301-redirects into the Coda help centre and the target article returned HTTP 403 to an unauthenticated fetch. Treat Coda Brain / Grammarly as unassessed in this comparison.
Onyx repo metrics: 31,998 stars, 4,408 forks, created 2023-04-27, last pushed 2026-09-09, dual-licensed (MIT Community Edition + Enterprise Edition). Dust: 1,459 stars, MIT, created 2022-08-19.

Microsoft ships an agent governance plane (Agent 365 / agent registry in the M365 admin center) covering onboarding approval, least-privilege access to users/data/tools, rules-based lifecycle policies including flagging ownerless agents, and audit-readiness — a moat GBrain has no equivalent for.

gaps.recommendation: Answer the "this is enterprise KM renamed" objection in the synthesis with a concession-then-fork structure, not a denial. Concede three points outright with primary-source citations: Glean/Notion/Dust all ship SKILL.md-based procedural memory (Dust's nightly Self Improving Skills is GBrain's skillopt shipped by a competitor), Guru's automated verify/unverify is more automated write-side curation than GBrain's, and MCP is universal. Then locate the real difference in ONE architectural fact: incumbents are an index over sources (source app stays authoritative, index is disposable), a company brain is a new writable system of record. That single inversion is what makes per-fact provenance, temporal supersession, decay, forget and a diffable audit trail possible, and it is why R4 (contradiction arbitration) is structurally unavailable to incumbents rather than merely unbuilt — verified by 0/1,402 Glean doc pages, 0 in the Microsoft docs repo, 0 in Dust. Keep the ranked "what it adds" list to four items (per-fact provenance in an owned store; contradiction detection that refuses to auto-resolve; a SHARED org hot-to-cold loop, since every incumbent memory is per-user; and ownership/exit via MIT+markdown+git+MEMORY_VERBS), strike skills and MCP from it, and attach the C1 caveat that none of the first three has a measured end-to-end win. State the ACL gap using Tan's own sentence from docs/tutorials/company-brain.md ("Read scoping stays source-granular in both models") rather than the stale May-2026 "no multi-tenancy" critiques, which the September release has partly overtaken — the honest claim is source-granular vs document-granular, a category difference. Use Onyx's 11-of-52 connectors / EE-only / 5-30 minute sync numbers to show permission mirroring is a per-connector fleet, not a sprint, and use Microsoft's admission that Purview retention and audit logging do not apply to Copilot memory to reframe the gap as "agent-written memory is an unsolved governance category industry-wide" rather than a GBrain oversight. Carry two things into the design and judging phases: (1) the strongest counter-argument to our own thesis — Glean already imports GitHub skills and mirrors ACLs, so shipping per-fact provenance plus a contradiction probe would collapse three of our four differentiators in one release; the window is narrow; and (2) the crux experiment, which is cheap and unrun by anyone: same corpus, same top-k, same reranker, Glean/Onyx-class hybrid vs a curated brain, scored on LongMemEval-S knowledge-update and conflict slices, where the thesis predicts incumbents fail on exactly those two slices and tie elsewhere. Flag two coverage holes for a follow-up worker with search budget: Coda Brain/Grammarly is unassessed (403), and the 2026 entrants (Hyper, Memory Store, Almanac, Hyperspell, Savant, Within) are carried over from prior reports rather than verified here.

key_insights: Tan's two uses of 'librarian' are two distinct professions with separate literatures, which dissolves contradiction C2: Sense A (hygiene/pruning) is COLLECTION MANAGEMENT (appraisal, weeding, retention, deaccessioning); Sense B ('picks the three books') is REFERENCE SERVICE. GBrain — and every memory system in this corpus — is excellent at Sense B and completely unstaffed at Sense A. gbrain-architecture.md described Sense B machinery and labelled it Sense A.

The highest-value transfer from library science is a CONTROL LAW, not a threshold. CREW: 'you should weed about the same amount as you are adding to the collection.' Slaving weed rate to acquisition rate turns pruning from an unbounded judgment problem into a bounded ranking problem (rank by weed score, truncate the queue at N = pages added this period). This structurally cannot produce GBrain's observed failure: take_proposals reaching 32,500 rows and growing 2,000-6,000/day (gbrain#3269), because that queue was a filter with no budget.

OAIS states the exact invariant and GBrain satisfies only half of it. CCSDS 650.0-M-2 §3.1 requires an archive to follow documented policies 'ensuring that it is never deleted unless allowed as part of an approved strategy. There should be no ad-hoc deletions.' 'No ad-hoc deletions' presupposes an approved disposal SCHEDULE. GBrain has the prohibition and no schedule — v06b verified there is no knowledge-retention config key at all. That is the precise shape of the gap, and it reframes the critique: refusing to auto-delete is correct curatorial posture; never building the schedule/policy/authority that lets a human delete cheaply is the defect.

GBrain already collects the exact signal CREW weeds on and spends it on the opposite function. I verified directly at src/schema.sql:122-126 and 270-276 that pages.last_retrieved_at exists ('NULL = never retrieved'), is fully B-tree indexed, and its sole consumer is gbrain lsd's stale-page query (last_retrieved_at IS NULL OR < NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days') — which selects never-read pages IN ORDER TO GENERATE MORE PAGES. CREW's second formula figure is literally 'years since its last recorded circulation.' The circulation desk is wired to the acquisitions department.

FRBR/IFLA-LRM would have prevented GBrain's hardest contradiction bug. The probe needed six verdict classes because, per its own RFC, it 'can't distinguish this changed from this is wrong' (~115 HIGH findings walked by hand). In bibliographic terms those are two EXPRESSIONS of one WORK related by succession vs. two Works in genuine conflict — a structural, not semantic, distinction. Arbitration belongs at the Work level on an SPO key; GBrain arbitrates at the Item level (chunk pairs), the one level where the question is undecidable. This converges exactly with MemStrata's 2026 result (cosine separates the two at AUROC 0.59; deterministic SPO supersession takes evolving-knowledge accuracy from 0.20-0.47 to 0.95-1.00).

Macro-appraisal (Terry Cook, National Archives of Canada, 1991) says the cheap high-leverage decision is at the SOURCE/function level, not the page level: appraise which company functions get documented at all. Cost model: macro-appraisal is O(channels), microappraisal is O(documents). GBrain's ~$0.0006/judge-call per document over a 155K-page brain is microappraisal without macro-appraisal. The sources table plus db_tracked/db_only is the right substrate and nothing uses it to stop ingesting anything.

Schellenberg's two-axis appraisal (evidential vs informational value) is directly actionable and fixes a modelling error common to every system in the corpus: scoring documents on one 'importance' axis. High informational / low evidential (transcripts) => synthesise then discard the carrier. High evidential (decision records, postmortems, board minutes) => keep verbatim forever even if never read, because it is the only proof the decision happened. GBrain's synthesize triage is a single number (threshold 0.5, rescue floor 0.30) and cannot express 'worthless content, irreplaceable evidence' — the class that matters legally.

Records with evidential or legal value must LEAVE the weeding system entirely and be governed by a retention schedule (NARA GRS model: mandatory, class-level, decided once in advance by an authority, executed with no per-item review). Conflating weeding with retention is how a company brain deletes the one document its lawyers needed. This also supplies the mechanism that makes deletion default and unremarkable — the missing half of 'no ad-hoc deletions.'

Authority control offers more than canonical strings: an authority record carries see references, SEE ALSO references, QUALIFIERS (dates/role/affiliation) and a CATALOGUER'S NOTE citing the evidence for the heading. GBrain has canonical slugs + alias hop only, and the predicted failure is exactly gbrain#4222 junk_entity_hubs — near-empty entity pages with 'generic-token names like Will' accreting huge edge counts from the regex auto-linker, surfaced as 'Warn + list only.' Refusing to auto-link unqualified single-token names is a data fix, not an LLM fix.

Ranganathan's Law 4 ('Save the time of the reader,' 1931) is the answer to 'storage is cheap, why prune?': you weed to protect precision and the reader's attention, not shelf space. In a company brain the reader is an agent with a token budget, so precision@k IS the reader's time — and this is Tan's own framing at 12:45 ('who decides which three books are open on that desk'). But note the disanalogy: physical weeding is FORCED by shelf space and a company brain has none, so it will not weed unless the rate law is enforced deliberately. That argues for scheduled disposal as the primary mechanism and human weeding as the exception — inverting the emphasis of the physical-library literature.

key_facts.claim: CREW = Continuous Review, Evaluation, and Weeding. Its formula has three parts: first figure = years since latest copyright date (content age); second figure = maximum permissible time without usage, i.e. 'years since its last recorded circulation'; third = presence of MUSTIE factors. Worked example given verbatim: '8/3/MUSTIE'. 'X' fills any part not applicable to a class.

MUSTIE expands verbatim to: Misleading (and/or factually inaccurate); Ugly (worn and beyond mending or rebinding); Superseded (by a truly new edition or by a much better book on the subject); Trivial (of no discernible literary or scientific merit; usually of ephemeral interest at some time in the past); Irrelevant to the needs and interests of your community; the material or information may be obtained expeditiously Elsewhere.

CREW's rate law and cadence: 'you should weed about the same amount as you are adding to the collection unless you are in a developing mode'; 'about 5% of the collection be weeded every year' (citing Slote, Weeding Library Collections, 1997, p.14), which 'allows for turnover of the collection every twenty years'; weekly staff pulls of shabby/outdated items; quarterly catalogue reports to identify 'shelf sitters'; monthly targets for specific collection areas; and 'the entire collection should be reviewed and weeded if necessary, at least once every five years.'

Observed CREW formula distribution across Dewey classes in the 2012 manual: 10/3/MUSTIE x17, 5/3/MUSTIE x15, X/3/MUSTIE x7, 5/2/MUSTIE x6, X/2/MUSTIE x4, plus singletons including 15/5/MUSTIE and X/1/MUSTIE. The manual notes 'Most formulas include a 3 in the usage category because few libraries can afford to keep items in the collection that have not circulated or been used in-house within a three year period' — i.e. the age figure varies widely by class, the use figure barely does.

CREW's disposal slip (final page) is a closed-set form: Bindery / Discard / Mend-Preserve / Book Sale / Promote / Replacement-New Edition / Donate to / Sent To, plus a mandatory 'Check Database for other locations of this title' pre-check and a named 'Authorizing Agent' signature line.

The Texas State Library and Archives Commission has archived the CREW Manual with no plans to update it; the live page now only offers to email an archived copy. The 2012 edition (rev. Jeanette Larson, 107 pp., CC BY-NC-ND 3.0) is retrievable from the Internet Archive.

SAA's Guidelines for Reappraisal and Deaccessioning (approved by SAA Council, May 2012) distinguish three operations: weeding ('identifying and removing unwanted materials from a larger body of materials'), deaccessioning ('permanently removes accessioned materials ... Note: This is not to be confused with weeding'), and reappraisal ('identifying materials that no longer merit preservation and that are candidates for deaccessioning'). Hard rule: 'Reappraisal does not always lead to deaccessioning. However, reappraisal is required as a first step towards any specific act of deaccessioning.'

SAA makes a written collecting policy the precondition for any disposal decision: 'It is impossible to make accurate and defensible deaccession decisions if it is not clear what the repository seeks to acquire in the first place.' A separate collection management policy must define 'the authority and approval processes for deaccessioning decisions; identifying acceptable methods of disposal ... and identifying a process for dealing with collections with unknown provenance,' be formally approved by administration and made public. Every step must be documented and retained as a permanent administrative record, and 'Never should reappraisal and deaccessioning be done secretly or under the table.'

SAA's reappraisal decision criteria include: contents/subject unknown, does not fit the current collecting policy, no catalog records, provenance unknown, 'have not been used or their use is extremely infrequent', not unique, highly restricted, transactional records with no long-term research value, not the record copy, unprocessed and offsite for long periods. The four disposition options after a deaccession decision are transfer, return to donor, sale, and destruction. Deferment is explicitly warned against: it 'should not become an easy excuse for continuing to do nothing with a backlogged collection.'

OAIS (CCSDS 650.0-M-2, June 2012, = ISO 14721:2012) mandates that an archive 'Follow documented policies and procedures which ensure that the information is preserved against all reasonable contingencies, including the demise of the Archive, ensuring that it is never deleted unless allowed as part of an approved strategy. There should be no ad-hoc deletions.' It also requires the archive to determine a Designated Community and ensure information is 'Independently Understandable' to it 'without needing special resources such as the assistance of the experts who produced the information.'

OAIS defines six functional entities — Ingest, Archival Storage, Data Management, Administration, Preservation Planning, Access — and three packages: SIP (delivered by the Producer for construction/update of AIPs), AIP (Content Information plus Preservation Description Information, preserved within the OAIS), DIP (derived from one or more AIPs and sent to the Consumer on request). GBrain maps cleanly onto five of the six; Preservation Planning — the entity that monitors whether the collection still serves the community and plans disposition/migration — has no counterpart.

Schellenberg's appraisal frame, per the SAA Dictionary: records carry primary value (to the creator) and secondary value (to later researchers), the latter subdivided into evidential value — 'the value that depends on the importance of the matter evidenced, i.e. the organization and functioning of the agency that produced the records' — and informational value, 'the overall usefulness of the content of the records.'

Macroappraisal is 'an analysis of the functions of an organization to determine the relative importance of those activities and set priorities for documentation' (Brown 1995), pioneered by Terry Cook and colleagues at the National Archives of Canada in 1991; it 'shifts the focus in appraisal from the actual records (the product of creation) to their context of their creation (the process)' (Cook 2004), is 'a top-down approach based on functional analysis' (Lemieux 1998), and is 'followed by microappraisal to determine which records are kept permanently.'

Respect des fonds is 'the principle maintaining records according to their origin and in the units in which they were originally accumulated' (Posner 1940a), emerged in Belgium and France c.1840, requires respecting not only separation between fonds but their internal organizational structure (Jimerson 2009), and 'has become the main principle of archives administration.' The Prussian provenienzprinzip, refined from it, became the modern concept of provenance (Duranti & Franks 2015).

NARA's General Records Schedules are disposition authorities covering records that document administrative or support functions, and their use is mandatory: 'Agencies must use the GRS unless they can justify the use of an agency-specific schedule.' Page last reviewed 2026-06-12. This is the model for class-level, decided-in-advance disposition that requires no per-item review at disposal time.

The IFLA Library Reference Model (published January 2018) is a high-level conceptual reference model consolidating FRBR, FRAD and FRSAD, designed for linked-data environments. Its Work/Expression/Manifestation/Item stack maps onto a company brain as claim-or-topic / compiled_truth synthesis / markdown page-version / chunk-embedding row — and locates contradiction arbitration at the Work level, which GBrain lacks entirely.

VIAF combines multiple national name authority files into one service, 'lower[ing] the cost and increas[ing] the utility of library authority files by matching and linking widely used authority files,' drawing on more than 50 organizations from more than 30 countries, matching/linking/grouping contributed records into clusters. The transferable mechanism is the authority record's full structure: established form, see references, see-also references, qualifiers, and a cataloguer's note citing the evidence for the heading.

GBrain's pages.last_retrieved_at column exists with the comment 'v0.37.0 (migration v79): real stale-page signal for gbrain lsd ... NULL = never retrieved (LSD prioritizes these first)', and pages_last_retrieved_at_idx is a full B-tree index whose stated purpose is 'LSD's stale-page query WHERE last_retrieved_at IS NULL OR last_retrieved_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 90 days'. Verified directly at commit 43597b19, src/schema.sql lines 122-126 and 270-276. This is CREW's second formula figure (time since last circulation), collected and indexed, and spent on idea generation instead of weeding.

GBrain has no retention or TTL config key for knowledge content: a grep over KNOWN_CONFIG_KEYS returns only cache TTLs, an OAuth TTL, and memory.auto_writeback_transient_ttl (3d, on a default-OFF feature). Its per-kind fact half-lives (event 7d / commitment 90d / preference 90d / belief, fact, idea 365d) look like a retention schedule but decay.ts is a 'Pure function. No side effects. No I/O.' whose only consumers sort and print — so it is a read-time ranking penalty, never a disposal trigger.

GBrain's take_proposals review queue — the human-arbitration design's front door — 'reached 32.5k rows across ~2.9k pages, growing 2-6k rows/day' with the documented review CLI not actually existing (gbrain#3269, closed 2026-07-23, a week after the talk). This is the canonical failure of an unbounded proposal queue and is exactly what CREW's weed-rate-equals-acquisition-rate law prevents by construction.

GBrain's contradiction probe required six verdict classes (no_contradiction, contradiction, temporal_supersession, temporal_regression, temporal_evolution, negation_artifact) because, per its own May 2026 RFC, a production run surfaced ~115 HIGH findings whose hand-walking showed the probe 'can't distinguish this changed from this is wrong.' In FRBR terms that is a structural distinction (two Expressions of one Work related by succession vs two Works in conflict), not a semantic one, and it belongs at the Work level on an SPO key.

Ranganathan's Five Laws of Library Science — 1. Books are for use. 2. Every reader his book. 3. Every book its reader. 4. Save the time of the reader. 5. A library is a growing organism — are cited in the CREW manual (footnote 3: Asia Pub. House, 1963) as the grounding for weeding. Law 4 is the objective function that justifies pruning when storage is free; Law 5 is the counterweight against over-pruning.

Greene & Meissner, 'More Product, Less Process: Revamping Traditional Archival Processing,' The American Archivist 68:2 (2005), 208-263 — the 'golden minimum' processing argument, whose company-brain analogue is a minimally-processed lane that defers enrichment until first retrieval. The Allen Press article page returned HTTP 403 and the text was not read at first hand; the citation is standard but the paraphrase is unverified.

gaps.recommendation: Adopt library science's collection-management frame as the missing definition of "librarian," and state in the synthesis that Tan's word maps onto a profession with a published manual, a formula, a rate law and a cadence — which no memory system in this corpus implements. Use this sentence as the verdict on GBrain: it has built a technically excellent OAIS Ingest/Data-Management/Access stack with a rigorous no-ad-hoc-deletion posture, and has not built the approved disposal strategy that OAIS clause presupposes, so its librarian is a cataloguer and a reference desk with no acquisitions policy, no retention schedule and no weeding shelf. Present the five highest-leverage changes, all small diffs against GBrain's existing schema and none requiring a better model: (1) re-point the already-indexed pages.last_retrieved_at from lsd's idea generator to a weeding score and shelf-sitter report; (2) truncate the review queue at the acquisition rate (CREW's "weed about the same amount as you are adding"), which converts pruning from an unbounded judgment problem into a bounded ranking problem and structurally prevents the 32.5k-row queue explosion; (3) write three human-authored policy files (COLLECTING-POLICY.md, COLLECTION-MANAGEMENT-POLICY.md, retention.yml, ~2 pages total) without which no disposal decision is decidable and with which most disposals need no reviewer at all; (4) add a Work-level SPO key above the page so supersession is deterministic and the six contradiction verdict classes collapse to two; (5) add qualifiers and a cataloguer's note to the authority layer and refuse to auto-link unqualified single-token names, which eliminates the junk-entity-hub class at source. Route the specific artifacts to the design panel: the six-role human/agent split, the seven-tier cadence, the per-class A/U/MUSTIE+P formula table, the eight numbered decision rules with thresholds, the disposal slip with mandatory elsewhere-check and authorizing agent, and the nine metrics — of which M1 (queue clearance ratio >= 1.0), M2 (weeding rate / acquisition rate in 0.8-1.2) and M4 (shelf-sitter ratio trending down) are the three computable today from GBrain's existing schema. Two framings worth carrying verbatim into the synthesis: OAIS's "no ad-hoc deletions" means deletions must follow an approved schedule, not that deletions are forbidden — which reframes GBrain's refusal to auto-prune as correct curatorial posture with a missing second half; and Ranganathan's Law 4 ("save the time of the reader," 1931) is the profession's own answer to "storage is cheap, why prune," with the honest caveat that physical weeding is forced by shelf space and a company brain has none, so scheduled class-level disposal must be the primary mechanism and human weeding the exception. Flag two corrections for the corpus: MPLP is cited at medium confidence (article page 403'd, text not read first-hand), and the month values in the formula table are my adaptation, not empirically calibrated — they should be tuned against the stale-serve rate (M5).

key_insights: GBrain's access-control granularity is the SOURCE, not the document. Read grants are an array of source ids on an OAuth client (`oauth_clients.federated_read`); write grants are one source id plus an optional slug prefix (`bound_slug_prefixes`, server-enforced with `permission_denied`). GBrain's own company-brain tutorial states the ceiling: 'Read scoping stays source-granular in both models — within a shared source, everyone entitled to the source can read every folder.' There is no document ACL, no group model, and `facts` has no owner/user column at all — only `source_id` + `visibility ∈ {private, world}`.

GBrain's Row-Level Security is NOT a permission system and should never be cited as one. `docs/guides/rls-and-you.md` is explicit: RLS is enabled on every public table with ZERO policies, purely to deny the Supabase anon key via PostgREST; gbrain's own role holds BYPASSRLS; it uses ENABLE not FORCE; PGLite skips the check entirely. The schema's real ACL slot, `sources.config.access_policy`, is commented 'forward-compat slot, no enforcement in v0.17' and still has zero readers in src/ at v0.48.5.0.

The reference design for permission-aware retrieval already exists in open source and GBrain implements none of it. Onyx mirrors per-document `{external_user_emails, external_user_group_ids, is_public}` from 10 connectors, refreshes every 5–30 min, fails closed via `ExternalAccess.empty()` when permissions can't be resolved, namespaces principals (`user_email:`/`group:`/`external_group:`/`domain:`), and ANDs the querying user's ACL list into the vector query (ACL is OR-within, AND-with-rest per FILTER_SEMANTICS.md). Glean's Indexing API is the same shape. IMPORTANT MARKET FACT: Onyx's permission syncing lives in `backend/ee/` — the enterprise tree, not the MIT core. The one governance feature everyone needs is the one that is monetised.

Every mirrored-ACL system has a REVOCATION LAG equal to its sync period — Onyx 300 s (Drive/Slack/Teams/GitHub/Gmail) to 1800 s (Confluence/Jira/Box/SharePoint/Canvas); Glean warns of 'a small delay'. That, not 'we have ACLs', is the security property to state. Nobody has published a measurement of what actually leaks in that window — a good crux experiment.

A git-backed brain is erasable ONLY by history rewrite, and the erasure does not stay local. GBrain says so under the heading 'Honest forget semantics' (git filter-repo + force-push + re-clone everywhere). GitHub adds that data stays reachable by SHA-1 in cached views and in EVERY FORK, whose owners GitHub will not help you contact, and that removing cached views requires a Support ticket they grant only when credential rotation can't mitigate. Meanwhile GBrain's `forget` is a fence rewrite that KEEPS `~~the claim text~~` plus a `forgotten: <reason>` tombstone — retraction-with-audit, the exact opposite of GDPR Art. 17 erasure — and `page_versions` snapshots every page UPDATE with no TTL, so even the documented 'permanent' path (hand-editing the fence) leaves a copy.

The architectural fix is cheap and GBrain already ships the mechanism: DO NOT WRITE ERASABLE DATA TO GIT. Put anything person-identifying under a `db_only` path in gbrain.yml (auto-gitignored) and keep git for company doctrine. Erasure then becomes one DELETE transaction instead of a fork-coordination exercise. Caveat from GBrain's own docs: on PGLite the tiering is 'technically vacuous' — this requires Postgres/Supabase.

Two audit gaps are load-bearing. (a) `INSERT INTO mcp_request_log` exists ONLY in the HTTP transport — stdio MCP and local CLI produce no access records, and GBrain's own 'Model B' (one fat agent serves the whole team) runs on exactly those paths. (b) `summarizeMcpParams` redacts params to declared KEY NAMES plus bucketed byte counts, and no result identities are stored — so the log proves 'client X called recall at 14:02' and cannot answer 'did anyone see the performance reviews'. Plus there is no `DELETE FROM mcp_request_log` anywhere in src/: the retention sweep is a TODO, so the one audit table grows forever. OWASP's candidate risk for exactly this (ASI08 Repudiation & Untraceability) did NOT survive into the public-draft top 10 — traceability got folded away while poisoning stayed.

GBrain's guardrail seam CANNOT enforce anything, by explicit contract: `runGuardrails()` returns void, 'a guardrail registered through this interface cannot block, rewrite, drop, retry, or reorder GBrain behavior', every failure is swallowed (fail open), and 'GBrain writes no guardrail rows'. Against OWASP ASI06 — whose first mitigation is 'scan insertions for anomalies BEFORE committing them' — that is a detector, not a control, and it leaves no incident trace inside the brain. Enforcement must live in a quarantine wrapper upstream of `gbrain import`.

PRECISION CORRECTION for the synthesis: the corpus currently says 'OWASP lists Memory Poisoning as T1'. In OWASP's own repo it is ASI01 in the 0.5 initial candidates and, in the first public draft of the Top 10 for Agentic Applications, it is renumbered and broadened to ASI06 — Memory & Context Poisoning. 'T1' comes from the Feb-2025 Threats-and-Mitigations PDF's superseded numbering. Cite it as ASI06.

The mechanical trap nobody warns about: ANN indexes and ACL filters do not compose. pgvector's README states that with HNSW 'filtering is applied AFTER the index is scanned — if a condition matches 10% of rows, with the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, only 4 rows will match on average.' So a naive ACL predicate silently collapses recall for exactly your most narrowly-scoped employee, and the brain answers 'I have nothing on that' — indistinguishable from a genuine gap, so it never gets reported as a bug. It is a correctness failure before it is a security failure. Fixes: hnsw.iterative_scan=strict_order (≥0.8.0), partial indexes, or list partitioning.

The agent-memory landscape is far thinner on governance than the enterprise-search landscape: mem0's `user_id`/`agent_id`/`run_id` are documented as identifiers that 'scope the memory for future searches' with no statement about isolation enforcement — routing keys the caller supplies, not authenticated principals, so the security boundary is in the application. GBrain's OAuth-client scoping is actually ABOVE the median for this category (server-issued credential, federated_read threaded through AuthInfo, write scoping enforced); its problems are granularity and staleness, not absence of a mechanism.

A 25-person company does NOT get the GDPR Art. 30(5) small-organisation exemption. The exemption requires that processing be unlikely to risk rights and freedoms AND be 'not occasional' AND involve no special-category data. A brain that continuously ingests Slack, email and meeting transcripts is by definition not occasional. A one-page record of processing (including 'time limits for erasure') is the artefact that turns 'we thought about it' into Art. 5(2) accountability.

Recommended posture for 25 people: don't buy a permission system, buy a BOUNDARY. Three zones (OPEN / SENSITIVE / EXCLUDED) with default-deny at ingest, one GBrain source per zone, git for OPEN only and db_only for everything person-identifying, a weekly roster-to-grant reconciliation cron (GBrain's grants are registration-time snapshots that nothing re-syncs — this ~40-line job is the whole difference between 'we have access control' and 'we had access control in March'), a `brain_access_log` you own that records result_slugs and hashes the query text, and a 30/90/365-day retention schedule. ~2 engineer-days to stand up, ~2 h/month to run. Tripwire for building real ACLs: when the EXCLUDED list starts blocking work people legitimately need.

Two GBrain patterns are genuinely better than the field and worth copying regardless: (1) the 'write it in blood' RLS exemption — no CLI, only a psql table comment with a ≥4-char reason, re-enumerated by `gbrain doctor` on every run ('the escape hatch is not a one-time sign-off, it's a recurring reminder'); (2) provenance as a NOT NULL column with a `provenance_required` error, which satisfies two OWASP ASI06 mitigations at the type level. Also: the `coding-agent` preset's write-isolation-by-default into a throwaway `*-workspace` source is the correct shape for ASI03 and most agent stacks don't offer it.

FLY-SIDE BRIDGE that earns its keep on the company half: the write-time FlyHash novelty gate this project has been circling is ALSO the missing poisoning-defence primitive. ASI06 mitigations #1 ('scan insertions for anomalies before committing') and #12 ('flag abnormal memory update frequencies') are novelty-detection problems, and a novelty score at the `file_storage.markdown` seam gives a rate-limit signal on 'this principal is writing many near-duplicate records differing in one entity' — the observable signature of MINJA's progressive-shortening strategy. One cheap write-side gate serves both quality control and security.

key_facts.claim: GBrain's read scoping is source-granular, not document-granular: 'Read scoping stays source-granular in both models — within a shared source, everyone entitled to the source can read every folder.' Write scoping can be server-enforced per slug prefix (`--bound-slug-prefixes`, rejects with `permission_denied`).

GBrain's RLS is an anon-key exfiltration guard, not a permission model: RLS is enabled on all public tables with zero policies, gbrain's service-role connection holds BYPASSRLS ('enabling RLS without policies does NOT break gbrain itself'), only ENABLE is used (not FORCE), and the check is skipped entirely on PGLite.

GBrain's declared ACL slot is unimplemented: `sources.config` JSONB holds `{federated, access_policy}` and the schema comment reads 'access_policy: forward-compat slot, no enforcement in v0.17.' A grep of src/ at v0.48.5.0 finds no reader besides the schema comment and its generated copy.

GBrain's `facts` table has no owner/user column — scope is `source_id` plus `visibility TEXT CHECK (visibility IN ('private','world'))`. Identity in GBrain is 'which OAuth client', not 'which person'.

GBrain's `forget` is retraction, not erasure: it 'rewrite[s] the fence row with strikethrough + valid_until = today + context: "forgotten: <reason>"' and 'Both encodings keep the row in the markdown for audit history. To permanently delete a fact, edit the fence directly in markdown and remove the row.'

GBrain documents its own erasure limit under 'Honest forget semantics': 'The repo is git history — append-only. Deleting a line removes it from the working tree, not from history. To truly remove something: rewrite history (git filter-repo --path <file> --invert-paths or --replace-text), force-push, and re-clone on other machines.'

GitHub: removed data 'may still be accessible ... directly via their SHA-1 hashes in cached views on GitHub'; removing cached views and PR diff refs requires contacting GitHub Support, who assist 'only in cases where we determine that the risk can't be mitigated by rotating affected credentials'; and 'If the commit ... exists in any forks, it will continue to be accessible there ... GitHub cannot provide contact information for these owners.'

GBrain's MCP audit log is written only on the HTTP transport (`src/mcp/http-transport.ts`, `src/commands/serve-http.ts`); `src/core/surface-audit.ts` notes 'stdio ops don't otherwise log'. So local CLI and stdio MCP access produce no access records.

`summarizeMcpParams` reduces logged params to `{redacted: true, kind, declared_keys, unknown_key_count, approx_bytes}` — key names intersected with the op's declared schema plus a 1 KB byte bucket. No query text and no result identities are recorded, so the audit log cannot answer 'which pages did this principal see'.

There is no `DELETE FROM mcp_request_log` anywhere in gbrain's src/ at commit 43597b19; the retention sweep is a comment ('The retention sweep that bounds audit-table growth (Eng D8) lives in the autopilot cycle's purge phase, not here'), and `page_versions` (a snapshot per `pages` UPDATE) likewise has no TTL. Both grow unbounded.

GBrain's guardrail seams are observe-only and fail-open by hard contract enforced by test/guardrails.test.ts: 'runGuardrails() returns void. Callers never branch on a provider verdict. A guardrail registered through this interface cannot block, rewrite, drop, retry, or reorder GBrain behavior.' Also 'No verdict persistence. GBrain writes no guardrail rows.' The OSS distribution ships inert with zero providers registered.
GBrain has zero mentions of GDPR, right to erasure, DSAR/subject access, or legal hold anywhere in docs/ or src/.

Onyx's document-level ACL is `ExternalAccess{external_user_emails: set[str], external_user_group_ids: set[str], is_public: bool}` with `MAX_NUM_ENTRIES = 5000` ('not internally enforced') and a fail-closed `.empty()` fallback documented as: when 'some document's permissions aren't able to be determined (for whatever reason). Setting its ExternalAccess to "private" is a feasible fallback.'

Onyx mirrors permissions on a per-connector clock: default doc-sync 300 s (Google Drive, Slack, Teams, GitHub, Gmail) and 1800 s (Confluence, Jira, Canvas, Box, SharePoint); Salesforce gets post-query chunk censoring instead of a doc sync. This sync period IS the revocation lag.

Onyx's permission-syncing code lives in `backend/ee/onyx/external_permissions/` — the enterprise-edition tree with its own LICENSE — not in the MIT-licensed core. The repo has 31,998 stars and a top-level NOASSERTION licence (checked 2026-09-09).

Onyx applies ACLs as a query-time filter category: 'ACL | access_control_list | OR within, AND with rest', alongside a separate tenant_id category; `build_access_filters_for_user` computes the user's ACL entry list from Postgres per query. Principals are namespaced to prevent collisions: `user_email:`, `group:`, `external_group:`, `domain:`.

Glean's Indexing API models permissions as `allowAnonymousAccess`, `allowedUsers`, `allowedGroups`, `allowAllDatasourceUsersAccess`, with users/groups indexed separately and a `checkdocumentaccess` verification endpoint; enforcement is eventually consistent — 'permissions and memberships are processed asynchronously, there might be a small delay before documents are visible to groups / users in Glean searches.'

pgvector: 'With approximate indexes, filtering is applied after the index is scanned. If a condition matches 10% of rows, with HNSW and the default hnsw.ef_search of 40, only 4 rows will match on average.' Mitigations: `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order` (0.8.0+), partial indexes, or list partitioning. This is how naive ACL filters silently destroy recall for narrowly-scoped users.

pgvector on multitenancy: 'sharing an approximate index between tenants means vectors from one tenant can affect recall (and speed) for other tenants. For tenant isolation, use list partitioning or separate tables.'

Postgres RLS semantics: ENABLE gives default-deny but FORCE is additionally required to subject the table owner to its own policies; superusers and BYPASSRLS roles always bypass; permissive policies OR, restrictive policies AND; TRUNCATE and REFERENCES bypass RLS; unique/PK/FK constraint checks bypass RLS and can leak the existence of invisible rows; the planner may apply `leakproof` functions before the RLS check; `SET row_security = off` errors instead of silently filtering.

Pinecone recommends 'one namespace per tenant on a serverless index' for multitenancy — physical separation, no cross-tenant performance interference, near-instant offboarding by namespace deletion — and warns metadata-filter tenancy has 'significant performance and cost tradeoffs' (1 RU for a 1 GB namespace vs 100 RU to filter the same tenant out of a shared 100 GB index).

Qdrant recommends the opposite default from Pinecone: payload partitioning on a keyword index marked `is_tenant=true` (which co-locates a tenant's vectors on disk), and explicitly discourages collection-per-tenant — 'Creating a separate collection for each tenant is rarely the most efficient approach' — with a 1000-collection default cap per Cloud cluster.

MINJA poisons agent memory 'without assuming that the attacker can directly modify the memory bank' — only via queries and observed outputs, using bridging steps and a progressive-shortening indication prompt. The authors: 'MINJA enables any user to influence agent memory.' arXiv:2503.03704, submitted 2025-03-05, v5 revised 2026-02-12.

The follow-up study quotes MINJA at 'over 95% injection success rate and 70% attack success rate under idealized conditions' and finds that 'realistic conditions with pre-existing legitimate memories dramatically reduce attack effectiveness'; its two defenses (composite-trust I/O moderation; memory sanitization with temporal decay + trust-aware retrieval) require careful threshold calibration to avoid 'overly conservative rejection (blocking all entries)'.

CORRECTION to the corpus's 'OWASP T1' claim: memory poisoning is ASI01 in OWASP's 0.5 initial candidates and is renumbered/broadened to ASI06 'Memory & Context Poisoning' in the first public draft of the Top Ten for Agentic Applications. Its mitigation list includes 'scan insertions for anomalies before committing them', 'log all memory access and modifications', 'limit memory retention durations based on data sensitivity', 'require source attribution for all memory updates', and 'flag abnormal memory update frequencies'.

OWASP's candidate risk ASI08 'Repudiation & Untraceability' (0.5 candidates) targets exactly GBrain's audit gap — mitigations include 'log all delegation events with scope, originator, and receiver metadata' and 'implement deterministic replay systems for post-incident forensics' — but it did NOT survive consolidation into the first public draft, where ASI08 is 'Cascading Failures'.

OWASP LLM08:2025 names the multi-tenant RAG leak directly — 'embeddings from one group might be inadvertently retrieved in response to queries from another group's LLM, potentially leaking sensitive business information' — and prescribes 'fine-grained access controls and permission-aware vector and embedding stores', 'strict logical and access partitioning of datasets in the vector database', and 'detailed immutable logs of retrieval activities'.

OWASP Agent Memory Guard is an active OWASP project (Apache-2.0, 170 stars, created 2026-02-16, pushed 2026-09-09) providing runtime defence against memory poisoning: SHA-256 memory-integrity baselines, declarative YAML policies on memory read/write, snapshots + rollback, drop-in middleware for LangChain/LlamaIndex/CrewAI. It self-describes as the reference implementation for ASI06. Relevant to question (c) as a governance-side project built on these ideas.

GDPR Art. 30(5) exempts organisations under 250 employees from records of processing ONLY where processing is unlikely to risk rights and freedoms AND 'the processing is not occasional' AND involves no Art. 9(1)/Art. 10 data. A company brain that continuously ingests Slack/email/transcripts is not occasional, so a 25-person company does not get the exemption.

GDPR Art. 17(1) requires erasure 'without undue delay' on six grounds including 'no longer necessary in relation to the purposes'; Art. 17(2) requires a controller who made data public to take 'reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform' other controllers; the Art. 17(3) carve-outs are freedom of expression, legal obligation/public interest, public health, Art. 89(1) archiving/research/statistics, and legal claims. Art. 5(1)(e) separately requires storage limitation and 5(2) requires demonstrable accountability. (Text via the gdpr-info.eu mirror, not the EUR-Lex OJ original.)

mem0 documents `user_id`, `agent_id`, `app_id`, `run_id` as identifiers that 'scope the memory for future searches' — functional organisation, with no documented statement about isolation enforcement, cross-tenant access prevention, or security boundaries. The security boundary lives in the calling application.

GBrain retention knobs that DO exist: session transcripts 30 days (`dream.synthesize.corpus_retention_days`, 0700, outside the repo), stop-hook buffers 7 days, soft-deleted pages/archived sources 72 h then purge, `dream_verdicts` 30-day TTL, and per-kind fact-confidence half-lives (event 7 d, commitment/preference 90 d, belief/fact/idea 365 d). KEY_FILES.md is explicit that '`valid_until` is temporal validity, not retention' — decay reduces confidence, it never deletes, so knowledge itself has no retention schedule.

GBrain's content-level privacy control is genuinely good and is the one place it does better than source-granularity: a 3-layer strip means facts with `visibility != world` are stripped by the chunker BEFORE chunking/embedding so private text never reaches `content_chunks` or search results; `get_page` strips fences when `ctx.remote === true`; but 'Local CLI (ctx.remote === false) sees the full fence' — so the 'leak-free isolation across every read path' claim holds for the HTTP path only.

GBrain's read grants are static snapshots with no re-sync: the `daily-driver` preset's read grant is 'a snapshot of all non-archived sources at registration time ... a source you add next month is NOT automatically readable'. And the docs are honest that 'Rotation is not revocation — outstanding access tokens stay valid until they expire' (30-day default TTL on `agent register`).

GBrain's 'write it in blood' RLS exemption is a governance pattern worth copying: no CLI command exists ('A CLI command would make it easy for an agent to silently open a table to anon reads'), only a psql `COMMENT ON TABLE ... 'GBRAIN:RLS_EXEMPT reason=<≥4 chars>'`, and `gbrain doctor` re-enumerates every exemption by name on every run — 'The escape hatch is not a one-time sign-off, it's a recurring reminder.'

gaps.recommendation:
For a 25-person company brain, do not build a permission system — build a boundary, and make erasability an architectural property rather than a feature.

LAYER 0 — the boundary (half a day, do this first). Three zones, every connector/folder/page in exactly one: OPEN (safe if the whole company saw it) → GBrain source `shared`, `db_tracked`, in git; SENSITIVE (narrower than all-hands but valuable) → source `internal`, **`db_only`**, never committed; EXCLUDED (never ingested at any price) → HR files, comp, performance reviews, legal advice, board materials, candidate feedback, security incidents, DMs, private leadership channels, customer NDA material. Default every new connector and source to EXCLUDED and require a named human to promote it. The single highest-leverage decision in the whole design: anything *about a person* rather than *authored as company doctrine* lives under a `db_only` path, so erasure is one DELETE transaction instead of `git filter-repo` + force-push + re-clone-everywhere + a GitHub Support ticket + chasing fork owners GitHub won't name. This requires `gbrain init --supabase`; on PGLite GBrain's own docs call the tiering "technically vacuous".

LAYER 1 — identity and grants (half a day). One OAuth client per person (not per team): `--source <their write source>`, `--federated-read <their zones>`, `--surface starter`, plus `--bound-slug-prefixes partners/<slug>/` for server-enforced write confinement. Agents get the `coding-agent` shape (write to a throwaway `*-workspace`, read only what you name). Before handing out any credential, run GBrain's own isolation check — `gbrain init --mcp-only --force` on a scratch machine as that client, then `gbrain whoami` + a search for a known SENSITIVE string. Make it an onboarding checklist item; it is the only test that exercises the path teammates actually use. Set 30-day token TTLs; use `revoke-client` for offboarding, never `--reissue` (rotation ≠ revocation).

LAYER 2 — the reconciliation cron (~2 hours; the piece GBrain does not have). GBrain's read grants are registration-time snapshots that nothing re-syncs. Weekly: pull the IdP roster, `SELECT client_id, client_name, source_id, federated_read FROM oauth_clients WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`, diff, revoke any client whose owner has left, alert on any grant outside the zone table. Post the diff to a channel even when empty so a dead cron is visible (GBrain's own BRAIN_CURRENCY.md documents autopilot being dead 71 days behind three green dashboards). ~40 lines, and it is the entire difference between "we have access control" and "we had access control in March".

LAYER 3 — an audit log that answers the real question (half a day). Do not rely on `mcp_request_log` (HTTP-only, params redacted to key names, no result identities, no retention sweep). Add `brain_access_log(at, principal, transport, operation, query_hash, result_slugs[], zones[], latency_ms)` written at the retrieval seam. Three deliberate choices: store `result_slugs` (without it you cannot answer "did anyone see X before we pulled it", the only question that gets asked); hash the query rather than storing it (query text from a company brain is itself sensitive — this table becomes your most sensitive object the moment it's useful); record `transport` so you can see how much traffic bypasses the logged path. Then actually run the 90-day delete on both this table and `mcp_request_log`.

LAYER 4 — retention and erasure (half a day + an hour a month). Publish the retention schedule as an OPEN page so the brain can answer questions about its own rules: transcripts 30 d (existing knob), access logs 90 d, `page_versions` 365 d (needs a job — GBrain has none), SENSITIVE person-pages 365 d after last touch, OPEN doctrine indefinite, ex-employee pages purged at offboarding + 30 d. Write and rehearse one erasure runbook on a dummy person: `gbrain forget` (knowing it is a tombstone that preserves `~~the text~~`), hand-remove the fence rows per GBrain's documented permanent path, hard-delete `pages` so `page_versions` cascades, confirm nothing was in git. Keep a one-page Art. 30 record — you do not get the 250-employee exemption, because continuous Slack/email/transcript ingestion is not "occasional".

LAYER 5 — ingest and skills (half a day). Connectors write to `inbox/`; a policy step (secret scan, PII detector, novelty/duplicate gate, zone classifier) runs there; only cleared content moves into the synced tree. This is where enforcement must live, because GBrain's guardrail seam by explicit contract cannot block — register a provider for telemetry, but never mistake it for a control. Treat `SKILL.md` as the highest-privilege object in the brain: procedural memory that agents execute, so git + CODEOWNERS + human PR review, never an auto-ingest path. GBrain's `skillopt` no-regression gate is a quality gate, not a security gate — it will happily accept a malicious edit that scores well.

DELIBERATELY DO NOT BUILD at 25 people: per-document ACLs, group hierarchies, Drive/Slack permission mirroring, per-tenant index partitions, cryptographic provenance chains, a policy engine. All correct at 250 people, all maintenance sinks at 25. The tripwire that says build the real thing: when the EXCLUDED list starts blocking work people legitimately need. When that day comes, copy Onyx rather than inventing — `access_control_list TEXT[]` with namespaced principals, GIN index, entry list computed in Postgres and ANDed into the query, `is_public` as a separate boolean — and handle the ANN post-filter trap (`hnsw.iterative_scan = strict_order` or partition by zone), measuring recall for your most narrowly-scoped employee, not for an admin.

FOR THE SYNTHESIS, three things belong in the main narrative: (1) "Company brain" is currently a personal-brain architecture with a multi-user story bolted on — GBrain's ACL granularity is the source, its RLS is an anon-key guard with zero policies, and its declared `access_policy` slot has never been implemented; the honest sentence is "the 'brain' half is built and the 'company' half is a config convention". (2) A git-backed system of record and GDPR Art. 17 are not reconcilable by tuning, and GBrain's own docs say so — the reconciliation is the `db_only` boundary, which is the most actionable single recommendation this project can make. (3) Correct "OWASP T1" to ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning; and note that the fly-side write-time novelty gate this project keeps circling is simultaneously the missing ASI06 enforcement primitive, which is the cleanest point where the two halves of the user's question actually meet.

key_insights: The crux experiment is runnable today and is properly powered only if MemConflict is the statistical backbone, not LongMemEval. I downloaded and counted the released MemConflict set (Data/Step4_4.jsonl, 39.7 MB): 30 instances, 3,750 questions, 202K mean dialogue tokens per instance. Pooled with LongMemEval-S's 470 scored questions that gives n=4,220 and a paired-McNemar minimum detectable difference of 1.7-2.7 pp - enough to actually reject or accept a +/-2 pp equivalence band. LongMemEval-S alone detects only 5.0-8.0 pp, so every published 2-point 'win' on it is noise, and its knowledge-update slice (n=78) detects nothing under 12-20 pp and must be pooled, never reported standalone.

The primary endpoint has to be judged ANSWER accuracy with retrieval reported separately in the same table, because the two systematically diverge - MemConflict and gbrain-evals independently report this (95.53% retrieval completeness vs 86.6% answer accuracy on the same run). MemConflict's shipped diagnose_failures.py already decomposes errors into retrieval failure vs utilisation failure, which is exactly the split the crux question needs and is the single best reason to use that dataset over any other.

The protocol must forbid whole-system comparisons from producing verdicts. GBrain's own history is the cautionary tale: '+31.4 P@5' was a whole-adapter gap, re-measured by its own authors at +15.0 after a precision-denominator fix, and reduced to +6.2 R@5 / +9.7 first-place-hit when finally isolated with one switch (shared index, shared query vectors). So every arm runs an ablation ladder, and the decision rule carries an explicit RERANKER-EXPLAINED verdict - on the one dataset where it has been isolated, the cross-encoder reranker (+2.13 pp), not the graph and not the BM25+vector fusion (which is neutral-to-negative vs pure vector), supplies the headline gain.

The tuned baseline is where this experiment is normally lost, so tuning is specified symmetrically: same 30-trial budget, same dev split, same script, same reranker for baseline and treatment, with the full trial log published. Chunk size is explicitly pinned - MemoryAgentBench ran Mem0/Zep/Cognee/MIRIX at chunk 4096 while everyone else got 512 on a corpus of short numbered sentences, and that one uncorrected confound is why its Zep row (7% FC-SH vs BM25's 48%) cannot be used as evidence against bi-temporal graphs.

Arms split into an embedder-controlled family eligible for the primary test (tuned hybrid, GBrain default/graph-off/reranker-off, GBrain+FlyHash gate, Letta MemFS, full-context) and a black-box family that is descriptive only (Zep Cloud, Mem0 Cloud) - because you cannot pin the embedder on a hosted service, and pretending otherwise reproduces the exact error every vendor leaderboard makes. The full-context arm stays in: bounded self-managed memory loses 15 points to full context on knowledge-update questions with more capacity recovering nothing, and MemoryAgentBench v4's GPT-5-mini scores 78 FC-SH with no memory layer at all.

CARS is barred from the primary endpoint on its own authors' instruction. I verified the definition today from arXiv:2605.17301v1 III-E: CARS = 0.35*AC + 0.25*CDA + 0.25*RA + 0.15*SF, followed immediately by 'AC remains the primary metric; CARS is diagnostic only' and an admission that CARS 'structurally favor[s] systems with explicit conflict modules'. A curated brain beating a plain hybrid on CARS is close to tautological.

The real-org arm is buildable from what is already on this machine - 503 markdown files (3.68 MB) across 18 repos, 17 CLAUDE.md files, 39 MB of agent transcripts, and a genuine dated supersession chain in the auto-memory dir (the four NAS notes, where 'CMS package stopped' and 'healthchecks removed, dockerd writes down 95%' partially invalidate the earlier 'dockerd + CMS keep the disks spinning'). That is a real knowledge-update item nobody manufactured. Its honest power ceiling is 8-12 pp at n=200, which must be stated rather than papered over; its job is to catch large effects and the failure modes only a real corpus has.

Budget is modest and there is a decisive $30 slice. Full matrix: ~$770 reader + ~$20 judge + ~$116 full-context arm at Sonnet-5 rates, round to $850-900, ~3 machine-days mostly ingest. Tier-0 is MemConflict's 804 static + conditional questions (where newest-wins is inverted or undefined) across tuned-hybrid vs GBrain-default vs GBrain-reranker-off, one afternoon, MDD 5.7-7.4 pp - and nobody has ever run the file-and-git family on them.

key_facts.claim: MemConflict's released expanded benchmark (Data/Step4_4.jsonl, 39,671,712 bytes) contains 30 instances and 3,750 questions - mean 125.0 questions/instance, 202,050 dialogue tokens/instance, 52.6 sessions/instance - stratified as dynamic_conflict 2,946, conditional_conflict 444, static_conflict 360. The paper reports only 12 instances, so the public release is 2.5x larger.

CARS is defined as 0.35*AC + 0.25*CDA + 0.25*RA + 0.15*SF (answer correctness, conflict-detection F1, resolution appropriateness, source fidelity), and the paper states in the same paragraph that 'AC remains the primary metric; CARS is diagnostic only' and that CARS 'structurally favor[s] systems with explicit conflict modules'.

LongMemEval ships the baseline retrieval and full-context generation commands the protocol needs: 'bash run_retrieval.sh IN_FILE RETRIEVER GRANULARITY' with RETRIEVER in {flat-bm25, flat-contriever, flat-stella, flat-gte} and GRANULARITY in {turn, session}; 'bash run_generation.sh DATA_FILE MODEL full-history-session TOPK json false con' for the full-context ceiling; and 'python3 evaluate_qa.py gpt-4o your_hypothesis_file ../../data/longmemeval_oracle.json' as the official judged scorer.

GBrain publishes its own reproduction command for the reranker-off LongMemEval row: 'gbrain eval longmemeval <longmemeval_s_cleaned.json> --retrieval-only --top-k 5 --by-type --no-trajectory --mode balanced --reranker off --autocut off', which reproduces 93.40% strict recall_all@5 (439/470) against a sibling gbrain-evals receipt of 438/470 with 469 of 470 rows agreeing per question.

gbrain-evals exposes a four-method Adapter interface (init / query / optional snapshot / teardown) with gold stripped at the boundary, plus runnable commands: 'BRAINBENCH_N=1 bun eval/runner/multi-adapter.ts --adapter grep-only --queries relational' (free, no API calls) and 'bun run eval:run' for all question families. Its own eval README labels the 49.1%/97.9% graph result 'a historical pre-audit measurement' whose missing raw receipt and template-specific parser 'limit what it establishes'.
